”The Lord gave me a spaceship, he said come and visit me. It’s cheaper than living, but the journey isn’t free.” – E. Nichols

He slowly gasped for air with each wheezing breath through his oxygen mask as he lay on the hospital bed, the white sheet and blanket tucked snugly against his frail body. As I held his hand, I could feel the bones and veins protruding through his skin. He wasn’t the man he used to be, at least not physically. It had been a long year, but the cancer was finally winning. He knew it. I knew it. Alise knew it. She sat on the other side of his bed with her face in her hands, quietly muttering a prayer.

I had given up on God many years ago, but couldn’t bring myself to tell him. Why pray to a God who never listens, a God who takes the things you love most in life? God took mom last year. It was harder for dad, but he stayed strong. He kept telling us, “God has a plan,” that she’d find peace and he’d be with her again someday. But we could see the pain it caused him. That was before his diagnosis, long before that “someday” was today. Some fucking plan, huh.

He shifted his eyes toward me and gave me a weak smile. He tried to hide the pain, but I could see it as his smile turned into a grimace. I knew he was hurting. He squeezed my hand and released it, signaling with one finger to come close. I got up from my chair and leaned over him as he struggled to remove his mask.

“There’s something I’ve left for you.” He said in a hushed voice.

“Dad, it’s okay, we’ll take care of everything. Don’t worry about the stuff,” I tried to assure him. He shook his head dismissively.

“No, remember our old fishing hole? There’s a tall oak tree up the hill. It’s buried below the mark on the tree. You’ll know it when you see it,” He struggled with each word, but had a look of relief on his face when he finally got the words out. Alise lifted her head out of her hands and was watching now with a confused look on her face.

“What is it, dad?” Alise asked.

He shifted his gaze to her and smiled.

“Oh Alise, my baby. It’s my life. There are some things I couldn’t tell you kids growing up, but it’s time for you to know now.” He said as he turned his attention to her. Alise looked up at me and I back at her. We were both confused. What kind of secrets was our father keeping from us all these years?

“I want you to know, I love you both so dearly,” he said as his eyes watered and a single tear spilled down his cheek. We both told him we loved him too as the tears welled in our eyes.

Within moments the rhythmic metronome of his heart monitor transitioned from a pulsing beep to a single steady tone. It was the most chilling alarm. The signal of the end. As the nurses rushed in to tend to him Alise and I stepped back out of the way. I hugged her as she cried into my chest. We knew the nurses were just going through the motions to make sure he passed easily. There was no saving him and everyone knew it.

I spoke with the doctor and tended to the paperwork. Alise was in the waiting room being consoled by the nurses. It was hitting her hard. Having finished the paperwork, I walked over to Alise.

“We have to find it, whatever it is, by that tree,” She said as her voice cracked. I agreed, the mystery that was apparently our father’s life had to be answered. We got in the car and drove out to the river.

It had been years since I’d been back to the river. Dad taught me how to fish there and we spent many early mornings catching rainbow trout with our fly rods. He always said it was his favorite place in the world. I remember asking why at the time, but I can’t remember the reason. Alise and I walked down the wooded path to the riverbank where the woods opened up to the beautiful babbling shallows of the river. Not far from our usual fishing spot, I saw the lone oak tree, up on a small hill.

“I think that’s the tree,” I said as I pointed it out to Alise.

It was an oak tree. Nothing special about it at first, but Alise quickly found the mark Dad was talking about. There it was, a faint carving of a heart with our parents’ initials P+A, Paul and Anne. Below the carving was a large flat rock, the grass had grown up around it. I pulled up the rock, pushed it aside, and grabbed a nearby stick. Using the stick, I dug into the dirt. I didn’t know why I was digging, but it seemed the right thing to do.

I found it, whatever it was. The stick scraped against something flat. Each prod of the stick in the soil produced a hollow thump sound. I got down on my knees and began to clear the dirt out of the hole with my hands. Alise, hovering over me, leaned against the tree and observed from above.

It was a metal box of some sort. Finally I was able to remove the box from the moist dirt, knocking off the clumps as I tried to read the inscription on the lid. There were some strange writings etched into the metal lid. I first thought it was Chinese or some Asian writing, but then I noticed the symbols. It looked almost….ancient, like hieroglyphics. I grabbed the lip of the lid with my fingertips and pried it off. The lid had started to rust shut and it took more force to open than I expected. The lid flew off with a clank as it hit the tree and bounced into the grass. As I looked inside the box I pulled out the large square of folded paper that had been placed neatly on top of a cloth which covered the rest of the contents.

“What is it? What’s in the box?” Alise asked eagerly.

I unfolded the paper and began to read it silently to myself.

“What’s it say? Read it out loud,” she said.

I started over and began to read aloud what appeared to be a set of instructions written in dad’s handwriting. I paused after a moment, silently scanning over what I had just read. I couldn’t believe it.

“What the…?” Alise said as she grabbed the paper out of my hands and read it to herself in disbelief. We weren’t quite sure what to make of it. Was this real? Was this some sort of prank? Why did he wait until now to tell us about…. whatever this was?
